summary: The paper proposes Cascade-Aware Curriculum (CAC), a training scheme for tool-use LLM agents that orders training data by an estimated 'recoverability' score, injects synthetic recoverable faults at annealed rates and depths, and scaffolds self-check spans that are faded out over training. It claims 41â€“58% relative reduction in cascade-failure rate over vanilla SFT and 19â€“33% over the next-best baseline across three tool-use benchmarks, with multi-seed variance, oracle-noise quantification, and a reference-policy sensitivity analysis meant to address circularity concerns. However, the submitted manuscript cuts off mid-sentence at the start of Section 3.1 ('held-out test splits disjoint from curriculum construction data... data shuf'), so no actual results, tables, ablations, or the promised RL-baseline comparison, per-seed variance, or oracle-disagreement discussion are present in the text â€” only the abstract's summary numbers exist anywhere in the document.
strengths:
- The problem framing (path-dependent 'error cascades' vs. terminal errors) is a genuine and under-addressed failure mode in multi-step tool-use agents, and Section 2.1's operational definition of cascade vs. terminal failure via root-error step $t^*$ is precise and falsifiable.
- The recoverability score $R(t)$ (Section 2.2) is a concrete, estimable quantity (k=8 rollouts per injection point under a fixed reference policy) rather than a hand-wavy difficulty proxy, and the paper explicitly acknowledges and tries to test the circularity risk of using a model-derived curriculum signal (though the actual sensitivity analysis promised in Â§3.5 never appears in the provided text).
- The fault-injection taxonomy (F1â€“F5 across three depths) and the annealing schedule for both injection rate and self-check scaffolding probability are well specified and reproducible in principle, and the oracle-construction description for CodeDebug-150 (two-author agreement study, 91% exact match on 23 tasks) is a rare and welcome instance of quantifying labeling noise on a custom benchmark.
weaknesses:
- The submitted paper is truncated before any results are reported: Section 3.1 ends mid-sentence ('data shuf...') and there is no Section 3.2â€“3.6, no results table, no per-seed variance, no oracle-disagreement analysis for API-Orchestration-200 or ToolBench-Sub, and no reference-policy sensitivity analysis â€” despite the abstract explicitly claiming all of these were added in this revision. As submitted, none of the headline numbers (41â€“58%, 19â€“33%, 3.4%Â±0.6% compute overhead) are traceable to any table or method-of-computation in the body text; they exist only in the abstract.
- All three benchmarks use a single 7B base model with LoRA fine-tuning; the paper has apparently already been told (per the revision framing) that single-scale results limit external validity, but no multi-scale results are shown to address this â€” the abstract asserts variance/seed reporting was added but scale is still unaddressed.
- API-Orchestration-200 and CodeDebug-150 are both custom, author-constructed benchmarks (200 and 150 tasks respectively), and the paper's own oracle for CodeDebug-150 has a non-trivial 9% root-error-index disagreement rate between two human labelers on a spot check of only 23 tasks â€” a small sample for a noise estimate that the abstract treats as settling the concern. Combined with the missing results section, it is impossible to verify whether CFR reductions are real effects or artifacts of the custom oracle/curriculum construction being correlated with the evaluation metric.
- The outcome-reward RL baseline is motivated well in the introduction (sparse/terminal reward, credit-assignment difficulty) but, as with everything else, no actual comparison numbers or experimental details (algorithm, reward shaping, compute budget matching) are given in the visible text, so the claim of addressing 'the RL-baseline question' cannot be evaluated.
- Reviewers cannot verify reproducibility claims (curriculum scheduler, fault-injection taxonomy, oracle-construction protocol 'released') without seeing an artifact link, licensing, or repository â€” none is given.
questions:
1. The manuscript cuts off mid-sentence in Section 3.1 â€” can the authors supply the complete Results section (3.2 onward), including the actual CFR numbers per baseline/benchmark/seed, the reference-policy sensitivity analysis referenced in the abstract as Â§3.5, and the RL-baseline comparison?
2. How is the 3.4% (Â±0.6%) training-pipeline compute overhead measured â€” is it FLOPs, wall-clock, or GPU-hours, and does it include the k=8 rollout cost for estimating $R(t)$ on the full training pool, or only the incremental curriculum/fault-injection/self-check tokens?
3. For API-Orchestration-200, the oracle is described as noise-free by construction, but the mock APIs were authored by the same team building the curriculum â€” was any check performed for whether the mock environment's task distribution is itself biased toward faults the CAC taxonomy is designed to catch (i.e., a form of the circularity concern applied to the environment rather than the model)?
4. With only 23 tasks spot-checked for CodeDebug-150 oracle agreement, what is the confidence interval on the 91% agreement figure, and was a similar inter-annotator check performed for ToolBench-Sub's reference trajectories, which are reused from an external dataset rather than authored in-house?
5. Does the recoverability-based curriculum ordering (Stage A/B/C bucketing) hold up when $R(t)$ is estimated from a reference policy from a different model family than the one being trained, and if so, by how much does downstream CFR degrade â€” this is central to the circularity rebuttal claimed in the abstract but not shown in the truncated text?
